practice1.prompt: The folder you are running in holds four files. Move each one into a folder named after its extension, so photo1.jpg ends up in jpg/. Move them, do not copy them.

cases.name: the jpg landed in a jpg folder
cases.describe: photo1.jpg inside a jpg/ folder, unchanged

hiddenCases.name: the png landed in a png folder
the csv landed in a csv folder
the pdf landed in a pdf folder
the originals were moved, not left behind
hiddenCases.describe: photo1.jpg gone from the top folder

practice1.hint: Copying leaves you with two of everything, which looks organised until you check the folder you started in. The last check is the one that notices.

choices: The contents of every file in the folder
The names of the entries in the current folder
Only the files, never the folders
The full path of each file
questions.explain: Names only, and folders are in there too. That is why the examples test is_file() before touching anything.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson's rename script offer a dry run?
choices: It prints what would happen without changing anything, so a mistake is cheap
questions.explain: An automation bug does its damage at machine speed and across every file at once. A dry run is how you find it while it is still only text on screen.

questions.prompt: For a Path called p, `p.___` gives you '.jpg' including the dot.
questions.explain: It keeps the dot, which is why the examples slice it off with [1:] before using it as a folder name.

questions.prompt: Which of these belong in a script that changes files in bulk?
choices: A backup, or a dry run, before the first real pass
try/except around the part that touches each file
Printing what it did to each file
Running it on every folder at once the first time
questions.explain: The first three limit and record the damage. Starting everywhere at once is how a small bug becomes an afternoon of manual repair.

reflection-exercise1.hint: Say what kind of task is worth automating, and give one reason beyond speed.

reflection-exercise2.hint: Pick something you actually do more than once a week, and say which step of it a script could take over.
